readerTitle: Why the boring idea paid its owner first
caseNote: 가상 사례 (치과 대상 장부 정리 서비스, 소비자용 앱, 홈베이커리) · 모든 인물과 상황은 설명용
insight: 무엇을 시작할지는 아이디어의 새로움이 아니라 고객이 이미 돈을 쓰고 있는 곳과 그중 내가 이길 이유로 고른다.
misconception: 좋은 사업은 아무도 하지 않는 새로운 아이디어여야 하고, 경쟁자가 많은 분야는 피해야 한다.

sources.text: 소규모 창업과 시장 검증에 관한 일반적인 경영 원리 (기존 지출, 대안 비교)
모든 인물과 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례(Maya, Leo, 홈베이커)는 가상이며 실제 통계나 연구 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. 카드에 수치가 들어가지 않도록 유지했는지 게시 전 확인하세요.
"새로운 시장은 수요를 만드는 데 더 많은 시간과 자금이 든다"는 일반 원리로만 서술했습니다. 특정 성공률이나 실패율 통계를 덧붙이지 마세요.

cards.title: Why the boring idea paid its owner first
body: Maya and Leo quit their jobs in the same month. Maya started doing the books for dental clinics. Leo built an app for something nobody else offered.
Friends called Leo's idea exciting and Maya's idea dull. A year later, only one of them was paying their own rent from the business.

image.label: Two founders at desks: one with ledgers, one with a phone app
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 서류철과 계산기가 놓인 소박한 책상의 여성, 오른쪽은 반짝이는 스마트폰 앱 화면과 화이트보드가 있는 화려한 책상의 남성. 실제 브랜드 로고나 앱 아이콘은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which business pays its owner sooner?
body: Maya knows dental billing from her old job. There are already several bookkeepers in her city.
Leo's app helps people track household chores. No one sells anything like it, so he has no competitors. Which one is more likely to pay its founder a salary in year one?

options.text: Leo's app, because it has the market to itself
options.feedback: No rivals means no one to beat, but often it also means no one is paying for this yet. Leo must create the habit of spending before he can earn.
Clinics already budget for bookkeeping, so Maya only has to win some of that spending. She gives up novelty to gain customers who are ready to pay.

options.text: Can't tell. It depends on who works harder
options.feedback: Effort matters, but it can't replace a customer's willingness to pay. Hard work spent convincing people a problem exists earns less than hard work serving people who already pay.

cards.title: One sold into a budget. One had to create it.
body: Maya had three clinics signed by month two. They were already paying a bookkeeper. She didn't ask them to spend more, just to spend with her, because she understood dental insurance billing better than a general bookkeeper.
Leo got thousands of downloads and kind reviews. But households had never paid to track chores. They used a fridge note for free. After a year, few were paying.

image.label: Money flowing into one business, a dry pipe into the other
image.brief: 두 개의 파이프 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Clinics' existing bookkeeping budget" 파이프에서 동전이 Maya 쪽으로 흘러감. 오른쪽 "Households' chore budget" 파이프는 비어 있고 끝에 "$0" 라벨. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Start where money is already being spent
body: When choosing what to start, look first for **existing spending**: customers who already pay someone, or something, to solve this problem today.

Existing spending is the strongest early evidence of demand. It shows the problem hurts enough to cost money. Your job shrinks from "make people care" to "be the better option for people who already care."
Maya's idea wasn't better than Leo's. Her starting point was.

cards.title: Three questions before you choose.
body: Run every idea through these, in order:
list: **Who pays for this today?** Name the people and what they pay, even if it's a workaround.
**Can I reach them?** A list of real names beats a big market you can't get in front of.
**Why would they switch to me?** A skill, a location, a relationship, a narrower focus.
cards.callout: Maya passed all three. Leo failed the first.
cards.softwareNote: For software, the spending is often hidden in workarounds: staff hours, spreadsheets, or a clunky tool a team already pays for. If Leo had aimed at cleaning companies that pay managers to schedule chores, he would have had a budget to replace.

cards.eyebrow: A new way of seeing it
cards.title: Competitors can be good news.
body: Many first-time founders search for an idea with no rivals. But an empty market is often empty for a reason: nobody wants to pay.

Competitors prove that customers exist and spend. A crowded street of hair salons tells you people in that area buy haircuts. The real question isn't "Is anyone doing this?" It's "What are customers unhappy about with the options they pay for now?"

cards.title: Existing spending is necessary, not enough.
body: Some markets are full of spending and still bad bets. If every rival competes only on price, margins can be too thin to live on. If the spending is shrinking, you inherit a falling market.
And without a reason to switch, you're just one more option. Truly new ideas can work too. They simply need more time and money to teach customers to pay, which makes them a different kind of bet.

cards.title: Now it's a home baker.
body: A skilled home baker wants to turn her hobby into a business in a mid-size town. She knows about 40 parents through her kids' school. Which should she start with?

options.text: A new fermented dessert that nobody in town sells
options.feedback: It stands out, but no one has a habit or budget for it yet. She would spend her early months teaching people to want it.

options.text: Custom birthday cakes, marketed first to the school parents
options.feedback: Parents already pay bakeries for birthday cakes, and she can reach 40 of them directly. Her edge is trust and personal designs, not a lower price.

options.text: Cheap bread sold wholesale to local cafés
options.feedback: Cafés already buy bread, so the spending is real. But her only reason to be chosen is price, which leaves little margin for a one-person bakery.

cards.title: Follow the money customers already spend.
body: The safest first business wins a share of spending that already exists, with a clear reason customers should switch to you.
**Try it today:** take one idea you're considering. Write down who pays for this problem today, what they pay, and one reason they'd choose you instead.
